title: Database Designer
description: Learn how database designers translate requirements into entities, keys, relationships, constraints, and compatible schemas, using course enrollment as a worked model.
notes:
## Deciding what the system needs to represent

A database designer identifies the facts a system must represent and organizes those facts into a useful model. The work includes clarifying entities, relationships, identifiers, constraints, and the meaning of individual attributes. It begins with the requirements of the people who use the system. Choosing column types is important, but it is not a substitute for understanding what a record means or which combinations of records should be permitted.

Consider a fictional college planning a course-management service. Students can take several courses, and a course can have several students. Staff need to distinguish individual students even when their names match. They also need to know what counts as one enrollment and whether the same student can enroll in the same course more than once. These questions determine the model before any particular table declaration can be evaluated as correct.

The designer should make assumptions visible. A rule might come from current policy, a technical limitation, or an unresolved question. Those are different kinds of information. Writing an assumption down does not turn it into a confirmed requirement, but it lets stakeholders and developers review it before applications depend on it. Unstated assumptions are harder to detect and more expensive to change later.

## Moving from a conceptual picture to logical tables

A conceptual model describes important real-world concepts and relationships without committing to every storage detail. For the college, it might identify students, courses, and enrollment. A logical relational model then describes tables, keys, and relationships that represent those concepts. Physical design adds access and storage decisions, such as indexes, for the chosen product and workload. These viewpoints are connected, but they answer different questions.

For a deliberately simplified course-membership model, use students, courses, and enrollments. A student is identified by student_id, and a course by course_id. An enrollment connects one identified student to one identified course. If the stated rule allows only one enrollment for a given pair, the pair can form the enrollment's primary key. The designer must verify that rule rather than selecting the key simply because it is convenient to draw.

The relationship between students and courses is many-to-many. A junction table represents its individual links without adding a fixed number of course columns to each student row. Each enrollment references exactly one student and one course. A student or course may have no enrollments in this simplified model. Those minimum and maximum participation rules matter just as much as drawing a line between two boxes.

## Selecting identifiers and constraints deliberately

A key identifies a record within the model's intended scope. A person's name is often a poor key because different people can share it and one person's name can change. An assigned student identifier can provide a more suitable stable reference. Even then, define who assigns it, where it is unique, and how records from other systems will be reconciled. A technically unique number does not independently prove that two source records describe different people.

A foreign key can enforce the declared reference from enrollment to student or course. It protects the existence of a referenced key under the applicable rules. It does not decide whether that enrollment is permitted by every academic policy. Prerequisites, time conflicts, capacity, and approval requirements may involve additional constraints or application and transaction logic. The designer should identify those rules and their intended enforcement points rather than imply that two foreign keys solve all registration requirements.

Attributes also need clear definitions. A course title differs from a course code, and an enrollment date differs from a final completion date. Define units, allowed values, nullability, and the meaning of missing information. A blank-looking value in a spreadsheet can conceal several different situations. Moving it into a database does not automatically resolve those distinctions or establish which interpretation the application should use.

## Discovering the right granularity with stakeholders

A useful question is what one record represents. A course such as Introduction to Databases can be offered in several terms or to several groups, possibly with different instructors. If the system must track those occurrences separately, a course record alone is not the right grain for a student's actual class registration. A course offering can represent a particular occurrence, and enrollment can then refer to that offering.

This refinement explains why stakeholder review matters. If the designer consults only a short course list and never asks the teaching staff about offerings, instructors, and schedules, the initial model may omit relationships needed by ordinary work. A model can look tidy while describing the wrong real-world units. Review it with realistic scenarios rather than asking stakeholders merely whether a diagram looks professional.

Another example concerns department membership. A policy of one department per student creates a many-to-one relationship from students to departments if several students share a department. It is not automatically a one-to-one relationship. If students can later hold multiple department assignments, a junction relationship may be needed. Changes like this should follow a confirmed requirement and a compatibility plan, not an assumption that every possible future arrangement must be implemented immediately.

## Reducing anomalies without ignoring the workload

Normalization organizes relationships to address particular dependency and update problems. For example, copying a department's current name into every student record makes a department rename require many coordinated updates. A separate department record can provide a single logical source for that fact. The designer should be able to explain which dependency is being represented and which inconsistent states the chosen arrangement helps prevent.

Normalization is not a promise that every report becomes cheaper. Combining normalized relations can require joins, and different workloads have different read and write patterns. A deliberately maintained summary or other denormalized representation can be appropriate when its benefits are supported by evidence. Document which fact is authoritative, how the additional representation is maintained, and what staleness or inconsistency is permitted. Otherwise the optimization simply reintroduces uncontrolled copies.

Avoid using the phrase over-normalized as a substitute for investigation. A slow query can have several causes, and an extra table is not proof of a design error. Examine the requirements, dependencies, queries, and measurements. The designer, developer, and operator may all contribute evidence before choosing whether to revise the logical model, the query, an index, or another part of the system.

## Collaborating with developers and operators

The designer defines what the structure represents and which states are valid. The application developer implements the workflows that use it. A database administrator focuses on the deployed system's operation. These are responsibilities, not sealed compartments. A developer may reveal that a proposed relationship makes a required workflow awkward, while an operator may identify migration or access concerns that the initial design did not address.

Agree on the contract callers will rely on. This includes identifiers, column meanings, nullability, expected uniqueness, and relevant access boundaries. An application that assumes a relationship is mandatory can break when the database permits it to be absent. Conversely, a form that treats an identifier as optional can fail against a required reference. These disagreements should be resolved through the model and interface contracts rather than hidden behind ad-hoc exceptions.

Design work continues when requirements evolve. A proposed schema change needs an understanding of existing records, queries, imports, exports, and downstream reports. Renaming a column can be easy in isolation and still break several consumers. Preserving compatibility may require a staged change or a stable interface. The correct plan depends on verified callers and actual data rather than a diagram alone.

## Reviewing a design with concrete cases

Walk through ordinary and boundary cases. Can a student exist before enrolling? Can two students have the same name? What prevents a duplicate enrollment pair? How is a repeated course in a different term represented? Which references may be missing, and which must always resolve? These questions reveal assumptions that a list of table names often leaves unclear.

A good design review records the answers, unresolved requirements, and intended enforcement points. It checks both valid scenarios and invalid states the system must reject. The result is a model that developers can implement, operators can maintain, and stakeholders can recognize as a faithful account of their work. The designer's central contribution is this explicit shared meaning, carried consistently from requirements into the database's structure.

questions.question_text: What is the primary responsibility of the Database Designer?
options: Identifying the data to be stored and designing the conceptual/logical schema, such as ER diagrams and relationships
Managing backups and tuning performance of the running database
Writing the front-end code that displays student grades
Consuming the finished application as a naive user
questions.explanation: The notes define the Designer's role as identifying data and designing the schema, entities, and relationships.

questions.question_text: In the enrollment example, why does the Designer introduce a junction table `enrollments(student_id, course_id)`?
options: To correctly model the many-to-many relationship between students and courses without redundant columns
Because junction tables are required for every one-to-one relationship
To give the DBA something to back up separately
Because course columns cannot be stored anywhere else
questions.explanation: The notes explain the junction table is introduced specifically to model the many-to-many relationship correctly and avoid redundancy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is listed as a typical Designer responsibility?
options: Choosing primary keys, foreign keys, and relationship cardinality
Applying software patches to the DBMS engine
Handling connection pooling in application code
Checking grades through a student portal
questions.explanation: The notes list choosing keys and cardinality among the Designer's core responsibilities, distinct from DBA or Developer tasks.

questions.question_text: How does the Designer's role differ from the Application Developer's, according to the notes?
options: The Designer decides what tables and relationships should exist; the Developer writes code that uses those tables
The Designer writes all application business logic while the Developer designs the ER diagram
They are identical roles with different job titles
The Developer decides table structure and the Designer only tests the application
questions.explanation: The notes state this distinction directly: Designer decides schema shape, Developer writes code using it.

questions.question_text: Why must a one-department-per-student policy be reviewed if students may later hold multiple department assignments?
options: The new requirement can need a junction relationship and a compatible migration from the former many-to-one arrangement
One department per student always means one-to-one with departments
Existing single references automatically represent unlimited assignments
Schema changes never affect applications
questions.explanation: Many students may share one department, so the original relationship is many-to-one from student to department. Multiple assignments change the requirement and may need a junction relation.

questions.question_text: According to the notes, why might a Designer sometimes deliberately choose NOT to fully normalize a schema?
options: Because over-normalizing without considering query needs can require excessive joins for common reports, so a documented denormalization can be the right trade-off
Because normalization is only a theoretical concept with no real effect on queries
Because normalization is illegal in relational databases
Because only the DBA is allowed to normalize a schema
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly mention that over-normalization can hurt query performance, making deliberate denormalization a valid trade-off in some cases.

questions.question_text: A Designer builds a schema without consulting the professors who will actually use the course-management system, and later discovers courses can have multiple sections taught by different instructors. What pitfall does this illustrate?
options: Skipping stakeholder review, which risks missing real-world relationships during design
Over-granting SQL privileges to end users
A crash-recovery failure caused by asynchronous commit
A metadata drift issue caused by an undocumented schema change
questions.explanation: The notes specifically warn that skipping proper stakeholder review risks missing real relationships like multi-section, multi-instructor courses.

questions.question_text: Which statement best distinguishes when the Designer role is most active compared to the DBA role, per the notes?
options: The Designer is primarily active at design time or when the schema evolves, while the DBA operates the already-built system day to day
The Designer is active only after the DBA finishes managing backups
Both roles are active only when an End User submits a support ticket
The DBA is only active during initial schema design, and the Designer only during runtime operations
questions.explanation: The notes describe the Designer's work as design-time and schema-evolution focused, in contrast to the DBA's ongoing operational role.

questions.question_text: What does the grain of a table describe?
options: The color used in its diagram
Only the maximum text length
The physical age of the server
What one record in that table represents
questions.explanation: A course and a course offering represent different units. Choosing the correct unit is essential before defining relationships.

questions.question_text: Why record an unresolved modeling assumption?
options: Because writing it down proves it is true
Because every possible future feature must be implemented immediately
So stakeholders can review it before callers depend on it
Because it eliminates the need for a model
questions.explanation: An explicit assumption is reviewable. It must still be distinguished from a confirmed rule.

questions.question_text: A student can take several courses and a course can contain several students. Which simplified structure represents the links?
options: A junction relation enrollments with student and course references
A single fixed course column on each student
A rule allowing only one student per course
One table for every possible student-course pair
questions.explanation: Each enrollment row records an individual link in the many-to-many relationship.

questions.question_text: The model permits at most one enrollment for each student/course pair. Which candidate primary key expresses that rule?
options: The student name alone
A nonunique course title alone
The pair student_id and course_id
The current display order of records
questions.explanation: The pair identifies one permitted membership link under the stated simplified rule.

questions.question_text: Two students share the same name. What should the model avoid assuming?
options: That students can ever have identifiers
That duplicate names require deleting a person
That a unique key must be a display label
That name alone necessarily identifies one student
questions.explanation: Human names are not guaranteed unique or stable. The identifier policy must fit the represented entities.

questions.question_text: A course runs in two terms with different instructors. What must the designer investigate?
options: Whether every course title must become a password
Whether terms can be ignored without stakeholder review
Whether every student must have the same instructor
Whether a separate course-offering entity is required
questions.explanation: The system may need to distinguish actual occurrences rather than only the abstract course.

questions.question_text: Many students belong to one department, and each student currently has one department. What relationship is this from students to departments?
options: Automatically one-to-one
Many-to-one
Many-to-many by definition
A relationship that cannot be modeled
questions.explanation: Several student records can reference the same department even when each student has only one such reference.

questions.question_text: The institution begins allowing multiple department assignments per student. What should happen?
options: Assume the old single reference can represent every assignment
Review the new requirement and plan a compatible relationship change
Change production data without inspecting callers
Claim the original policy was always many-to-many
questions.explanation: A confirmed policy change can require a junction relationship and migration/caller planning.

questions.question_text: An enrollment row references existing student and course keys. What do those references not prove by themselves?
options: That the referenced keys exist under the declared rule
That all capacity, prerequisite, and approval rules were satisfied
That relationships can be represented relationally
That the database can check a reference
questions.explanation: Foreign keys enforce their declared relationships, not every business condition of registration.

questions.question_text: A department name is copied into thousands of student records. What design concern should be examined?
options: The dependency and update anomalies created by multiple copies of one fact
Whether every student must now have a unique department
Whether copying automatically makes every rename atomic
Whether data meanings no longer matter
questions.explanation: A single logical department record can reduce the need to coordinate repeated copies of the current name.

questions.question_text: A maintained summary makes a measured report cheaper. Which responsibility accompanies that design?
options: Assume the summary never needs updating
Discard all source records automatically
Define its authoritative source, maintenance rule, and permitted staleness
Claim every normalized design is wrong
questions.explanation: Controlled additional representations require explicit consistency and ownership rules.

questions.question_text: Which review most directly tests whether the model fits ordinary college work?
options: Walking through realistic enrollment, missing-reference, and repeat-offering cases
Approving only the diagram's visual style
Choosing the shortest possible table names
Ignoring the people who use the service
questions.explanation: Concrete allowed and denied scenarios expose requirements that a tidy picture can omit.

diagrams.caption: A simplified student-course membership schema
diagrams.description: Each enrollment references exactly one student and one course. A student or course may have zero or many enrollments. The composite enrollment key permits at most one row for each student/course pair; real term-specific registrations may require an offering entity.
